summary: A country on the eastern half of the island of Timor in Southeast Asia, formerly a Portuguese colony, occupied by Indonesia after 1975 and formally independent in 2002, the first newly independent country of the 21st century.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Portuguese Dominican friars came to Timor to preach in the 16th century, but even when Portugal withdrew in 1975, Catholics made up only about 30 percent of the population. After the Indonesian invasion in 1975, the Indonesian government required citizens to register under an officially recognized religion, traditional belief was not recognized, and the church was the only institution able to protect the Timorese; from 1981 it held Mass in Tetum, and Bishop Belo, together with Ramos-Horta, was awarded the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize for this. Catholicism thus became a symbol of national resistance, and the share of believers soared to more than 90 percent.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: Protestantism arrived mainly during the Indonesian occupation of 1975–1999 with Indonesian immigrants and Indonesian Protestant churches, and some Timorese also joined. After the 1999 independence referendum many Indonesian immigrants left, and with Catholicism so closely tied to national identity, the number of Protestant believers is small.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: The history of Islam goes back to descendants of traders from Arabia and Indonesia, and the capital, Dili, has a long-established Muslim community. During the Indonesian occupation large numbers of Muslim immigrants came to East Timor, but after the violence provoked by the 1999 independence referendum most returned to Indonesia, so Muslims are now a very small minority.

religion.background: The indigenous people of East Timor believe in ancestral spirits and sacred sites, and the sacred house (uma lulik) is the center linking the family with its ancestors. From the 16th century Portuguese missionaries brought Catholicism, but converts were limited during the colonial period. During the Indonesian occupation of 1975–1999 the Catholic Church protected the people and documented human rights abuses, becoming an important force in the resistance movement, and the share of believers rose greatly. After independence in 2002 the Catholic Church has had great influence in society, and when Pope Francis visited in 2024 he drew about half the national population to Mass.

language.official: The official languages are Tetum and Portuguese, and Indonesian and English are working languages.

ranking.name: Tetum
ranking.description: Tetum belongs to the Austronesian family and was originally a regional language of central Timor. During the Portuguese colonial period the Tetum of the Dili area absorbed a great deal of Portuguese vocabulary and became the lingua franca among the various peoples. During the Indonesian occupation the church held Mass in Tetum, making it a symbol of national identity, and the 2002 constitution made it one of the official languages; about 40 percent have it as their mother tongue, but most citizens can use it.

ranking.name: Portuguese
ranking.description: Portuguese is the language of administration and the church brought by Portuguese colonization from the 16th century; after the Indonesian invasion in 1975 its use was banned, and the resistance organizations used Portuguese as a secret language of communication. At independence in 2002 the leadership chose Portuguese as an official language to link with the Lusophone world and set the country apart from Indonesia. But because a whole generation was interrupted, very few people have Portuguese as a mother tongue, and it is now being promoted again through school education.

ranking.name: Indonesian
ranking.description: Indonesian was the only language of schools and administration during the Indonesian occupation of 1975–1999, so a whole generation educated in that period can use it fluently. After independence the constitution made it a working language, and Indonesian television programs and goods keep it influential in daily life, but very few people have it as a mother tongue.

language.history: East Timor has more than a dozen indigenous languages, belonging to the Austronesian and Papuan families, and Tetum is the most widespread lingua franca among them. During the Portuguese colonial period (from the 16th century to 1975) Portuguese was the official language and was blended heavily into Tetum. During the Indonesian occupation of 1975–1999 Indonesian became the language of education and Portuguese was banned. After independence in 2002 Tetum and Portuguese were made the official languages and Indonesian and English working languages, and the language policy is still debated today.

ranking.name: Batar da'an (corn and pumpkin stew)
ranking.description: A thick stew of corn kernels, pumpkin and mung beans or other legumes cooked together for a long time, mild and slightly sweet, a common household staple in the mountains.
ranking.history: In Tetum "batar" means corn and "da'an" means cooked, so the name describes the method directly. Corn is native to the Americas and was brought to Timor by the Portuguese in the 16th–17th centuries, becoming the main food of highlanders because it suits dry mountain land. In the past, during the dry season and the "hungry season" before the harvest, this dish of corn, pumpkin and beans stewed together could feed a whole family on limited ingredients, and it is still one of the most common meals in the countryside.

ranking.name: Ikan sabuko (tomato and spice fish)
ranking.description: Pieces of mackerel or other sea fish are stewed or marinated with tomato, tamarind, chili and herbs such as basil, sour, fragrant and mildly spicy, often served with rice.
ranking.history: The north coast of East Timor faces the Wetar Strait, with abundant seafood, and fishing is an important livelihood for coastal residents. This fish dish blends native Timorese herbs, the Portuguese way of stewing with tomato and the sourness of tamarind in the Indonesian style, reflecting the history of East Timor's influence by both Portuguese and Indonesian cultures. It is common in homes and restaurants in Dili and is a representative seafood dish of East Timor.

ranking.name: Feijoada (bean stew)
ranking.description: A rich stew of beans cooked for a long time with pork and sausage and seasoned with tomato, onion and garlic, often eaten with rice or corn.
ranking.history: Feijoada comes from Portugal and developed into a national dish in Portuguese-speaking regions such as Brazil. Portugal colonized Timor for more than four hundred years and brought dishes such as feijoada into local homes, and the Timorese adjusted the ingredients to local produce. Because feijoada takes time and uses a good deal of meat, it is usually made only at festivals such as Christmas and at weddings, and it also symbolizes East Timor's cultural ties with the Community of Portuguese-Speaking Countries.

ranking.name: Timor coffee
ranking.description: Arabica coffee grown in the Timorese highlands, mostly cultivated organically, with a mellow body and aromas of chocolate and nuts.
ranking.history: The Portuguese introduced coffee to Timor in the 19th century and developed plantations in the western highlands in places such as Ermera. The "Timor Hybrid," a natural cross of Arabica and Robusta discovered in Timor in the early 20th century, is resistant to coffee leaf rust and was later widely used to breed disease-resistant coffee varieties around the world. Today coffee is East Timor's most important export apart from oil, and tens of thousands of smallholder families live from it.

ranking.name: Cassava (ai-farina)
ranking.description: Cassava is a starchy tuberous root that can be boiled, roasted, fried or ground into flour for cakes and snacks, with a creamy texture, and is one of the important staples.
ranking.history: Cassava is native to Brazil and was carried by the Portuguese to Africa and Asia after the 16th century and then to Timor; the "farina" in the name "ai-farina" comes from the Portuguese "farinha" (flour). Cassava tolerates drought and poor soil and provides food security when corn and rice harvests fail. In the war and famine of the early Indonesian occupation, many Timorese who fled into the mountains survived on root crops such as cassava.
